articles.title: Todd Haynes and Wallace Shawn among signatories of letter backing Mark Ruffalo amid antisemitism charge
articles.summary: More than 170 Jewish artists, also including Joel Coen, Hannah Einbinder and Miranda July, have supported the actor after he criticized Paramount. A collective of more than 170 prominent Jewish artists and academics – including Todd Haynes, Joel Coen, Miranda July, Hannah Einbinder, Wallace Shawn…
body: The actor had been accused of invoking antisemitic tropes after he criticized Paramount Skydance, the media company owned by David Ellison, a Donald Trump ally. Ruffalo had spoken out about the $111bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD).

In a statement posted to social media last week, the actor had highlighted the links between Paramount Skydance, poised to become one of the biggest media conglomerates in the US pending a court decision, and Oracle, the technology company owned by Ellison’s father, Larry, that has long supplied software to the Israel Defense Forces and government. Paramount responded to Ruffalo, saying it was “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute”.

The letter, titled “Enough!”, dismisses the accusation against Ruffalo as part of an “outrageous smear campaign” and calls for the end to “the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism against those who are brave enough to point out the obvious: that the assault on the Palestinian people and the assault on our liberties at home are deeply interconnected, and there is nothing antisemitic about recognizing that fact”.

articles.title: Ariana Grande Tears Up as She Ends ‘Eternal Sunshine’ Tour Ahead of Step Back From Visibility: ‘I Have Loved Every Minute of This’
articles.summary: Ariana Grande took a moment during the final show of her “Eternal Sunshine” tour to thank the audience at London’s O2 Arena, sharing how it’s been an “extraordinary experience” across her 41 shows. “I just want to say thank you so much,” said Grande, seated on a stool on the B-stage.
body: Grande kicked off her “Eternal Sunshine” tour in June with a trio of shows at Oakland Arena in California. Throughout the North American trek, she performed a handful of shows in various markets including Los Angeles, Austin, Atlanta, New York City, Boston, Montreal and Chicago. In mid-August, she traveled across the Pond for 10 shows at London’s O2 Arena, where she brought the journey to a close on Tuesday evening.

During the tour, Grande declared that she would be stepping out of the spotlight for an extended break following its conclusion. In early August, a rep for Grande cited “ongoing public scrutiny” as one of the reasons for the pause, and said that she “looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both happily and healthily.” In tandem, Grande bowed out of Stephen Sondheim’s West End revival of “Sunday in the Park With George.”

articles.title: ‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK
articles.summary: A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh. Occasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing.
body: Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town – Kenneth Rive’s Gala was a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese film Children of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planning a 75th anniversary series of screenings to showcase its history.

Such is Contemporary’s lustre that, along with screenings of films such as Miloš Forman’s A Blonde in Love, Bergman’s Wild Strawberries and Jack Hazan’s David Hockney documentary A Bigger Splash, the great and good are turning out in support, led by Mike Leigh, whose feature film directing debut, Bleak Moments, was picked up by Contemporary in 1971. “It was a great honour,” Leigh says. “One was used to seeing ‘Contemporary Films’ on all the movies one saw that weren’t just Hollywood crap.”

articles.title: Ariana Grande ends tour and steps back from public life
articles.summary: The star makes an emotional farewell as she wraps up a tour she's described as her "last hurrah".
body: Ariana Grande made an emotional exit on Tuesday night, as she wrapped up her Eternal Sunshine tour, and prepared to step back from public life.
The singer was occasionally close to tears - most notably during One Last Time, the song that took on extra meaning as an anthem for survivors of the 2017 Manchester terror attack.
"London, I'm going to need you to help me on this one," she said, kneeling down to be near the audience throughout the performance.
Last month, Grande announced a break from all future public-facing appearances following months of intense speculation about her health and appearance.

articles.title: Semi-pro football club 'in shock' after shirt worn by Reading Festival headliners
articles.summary: The club says sales of the shirt almost doubled after it was worn by Fontaines D.C frontman Grian Chatten.
body: A semi-professional Welsh football club say they were "in shock" after Fontaines D.C. singer wore their shirt during the band's Reading Festival headline set.
Lead vocalist Grian Chatten was seen sporting a green and white-striped Cwmbran away shirt during the performance on Friday, leading to pre-sales of the shirt to "almost double".
In a post shared on social media, the club said "we're still in shock and can't thank Grian enough for the support".
Sales of the shirt go both towards supporting the club as well as to grassroots music venues, with the club having partnered with four famous bands for their 2026/27 season team kits.

articles.title: ‘Led us down such a dark path’: documentary explores how 9/11 changed America
articles.summary: In Netflix film Turning Point: Generation 9/11, the lives of people forever impacted by the terrorist attack in 2001 are explored. Twenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history.
body: “When I do that math, I get to the bomb at Hiroshima – that’s how distant it is,” says Brian Knappenberger, 56, director of a new Netflix documentary, Turning Point: Generation 9/11. “When we talk about the second world war, for our generation it seemed like a long time ago but, for the current generation of 20-year-olds, that’s how long ago it was.”

Having previously made series about the “war on terror”, cold war and Vietnam war, Knappenberger felt compelled to address a generation for whom 9/11 is an abstraction they might find in a school history textbook, a solemn annual ceremony or, most disorientingly, a meme circulating on TikTok and Instagram.

Speaking via Google Meet from Los Angeles, he adds: “This film is coming from a place of respecting that experience, not assuming that people understand what it felt like to live through 9/11, which is so ingrained to those of us that did. It’s to illustrate not just what terrorism meant and how frightening that was but also how the decisions made in the days and weeks and years that followed – maybe more than the events themselves – changed us as a country.”

Twenty-five years on, memory is giving way to history.

articles.title: Super Nature review – crowd-sourced Super 8 film is a triumphant collage of hope for the natural world
articles.summary: Film-maker Ed Sayers’ project gathered footage from collaborators all over the world, cleverly edited to combine human and animal contributions. This delightful, fleet-footed film represents a labour of love both for its writer-director-producer-editor, Briton Ed Sayers, and his many, many…
body: The brief from Sayers was simply to film nature, so we get shots of all manner of flora and fauna, ranging from coral reefs to high deserts, places populated by minute bugs all the way up to whales. Given Super 8 reels can only capture a few minutes’ worth of stock, this must have been a fiendishly complex puzzle in the editing room, so all credit to Sayers not just for his own lovely footage and clever vision but for his nimble collaging of the whole thing together.

It is a work embellished by a sweet, swoony original score by Alexandra Hamilton-Ayres and some dainty Foley work (sound design is by David McAuley) to lay in, for example, the sound of two ibex butting horns. Super 8 cameras don’t record sound, and in fact one of the contributions comes from a British woman who has lost her hearing, and now finds communing with nature in silence all the sweeter.

articles.title: Ex-gang boss guilty of orchestrating 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was convicted over the drive-by shooting of the rap superstar 30 years ago.
body: Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.
The jury found him guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.
Dressed in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal.
During the trial, the court heard a recording of a police interview in 2008 in which Davis said he was in the car from which shots were fired, but did not himself fire the bullets that killed Shakur.
